title: Basic Botanical Nomenclature
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 100L Botany introduction to plant naming: binomial nomenclature, the International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN), taxonomic hierarchy, and rules governing valid scientific names.

questions.question: Who is credited with formalizing the binomial system of nomenclature used in botany today?
options: Carolus Linnaeus
Charles Darwin
Gregor Mendel
Theophrastus
questions.correct_answer: Carolus Linnaeus
questions.explanation: Linnaeus introduced the consistent two-part (genus + species) naming system in the 18th century, most notably in Species Plantarum (1753).

questions.question: In binomial nomenclature, a scientific plant name consists of which two components?
options: Genus name and species epithet
Family name and genus name
Common name and genus name
Order name and family name
questions.correct_answer: Genus name and species epithet
questions.explanation: A binomial is made of the genus name followed by the specific epithet, e.g. Mangifera indica.

questions.question: How should the genus name be written in a scientific plant name?
options: Capitalized first letter, in italics
All lowercase, in italics
All capital letters
Capitalized first letter, not italicized
questions.correct_answer: Capitalized first letter, in italics
questions.explanation: By convention the genus name begins with a capital letter and the whole binomial is italicized (or underlined when handwritten).

questions.question: How should the specific epithet in a scientific name normally be written?
options: Entirely in lowercase, italicized
Capitalized, italicized
In uppercase letters
Capitalized, not italicized
questions.correct_answer: Entirely in lowercase, italicized
questions.explanation: The specific epithet is always written in lowercase even if derived from a proper noun, and is italicized along with the genus name.

questions.question: Which body of rules governs the formal naming of plants, algae, and fungi internationally?
options: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)
International Code of Zoological Nomenclature (ICZN)
International Code of Nomenclature of Bacteria (ICNB)
International Plant Protection Convention (IPPC)
questions.correct_answer: International Code of Nomenclature for algae, fungi, and plants (ICN)
questions.explanation: The ICN (formerly the ICBN) sets the rules for valid publication and naming of plants, algae, and fungi.

questions.question: What is the correct standard sequence of major taxonomic ranks from most inclusive to least inclusive?
options: Kingdom, Division/Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Species, Genus, Family, Order, Class, Division, Kingdom
Kingdom, Class, Division, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Genus, Species, Family, Order, Class, Kingdom, Division
questions.correct_answer: Kingdom, Division/Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
questions.explanation: Taxonomic hierarchy descends from the broadest category (Kingdom) to the most specific (Species) in that fixed order.

questions.question: In plant taxonomy, family names are typically formed by adding which suffix to the stem of a genus name?
options: -aceae
-ales
-idae
-inae
questions.correct_answer: -aceae
questions.explanation: Plant family names conventionally end in -aceae, e.g. Fabaceae, Poaceae, Solanaceae.

questions.question: Plant order names conventionally end with which suffix?
options: -ales
-aceae
-oideae
-ineae
questions.correct_answer: -ales
questions.explanation: Orders in plant classification end in -ales, e.g. Rosales, Fabales.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the author citation that sometimes follows a scientific name, e.g. Zea mays L.?
options: It identifies the person who first validly published that name
It shows who first cultivated the plant
It indicates the collector of the specimen
It denotes the country where the plant was discovered
questions.correct_answer: It identifies the person who first validly published that name
questions.explanation: The author citation credits the botanist who validly published the name; 'L.' is the standard abbreviation for Linnaeus.

questions.question: What is a 'type specimen' in botanical nomenclature?
options: The single specimen permanently associated with a scientific name as its reference point
The most common specimen of a species in a herbarium
The first specimen collected in a new country
A specimen used only for DNA sequencing
questions.correct_answer: The single specimen permanently associated with a scientific name as its reference point
questions.explanation: A type specimen serves as the permanent reference that anchors the application of a name to a particular plant.

questions.question: What is a 'holotype'?
options: The single specimen designated by the original author as the nomenclatural type
A duplicate of the original specimen kept in another herbarium
A specimen selected later to replace a lost type
Any specimen matching the species description
questions.correct_answer: The single specimen designated by the original author as the nomenclatural type
questions.explanation: The holotype is the one specimen used or designated by the author as the nomenclatural type when the name was published.

questions.question: What term describes a specimen chosen as the new type when the original holotype has been lost or destroyed?
options: Neotype
Isotype
Syntype
Paratype
questions.correct_answer: Neotype
questions.explanation: A neotype is selected to serve as the nomenclatural type in the absence of all original material.

questions.question: What is an 'isotype' in nomenclature?
options: A duplicate specimen of the holotype, collected at the same time from the same plant
The second most important specimen chosen by a later reviewer
A specimen of a different species that resembles the type
A photograph used in place of a physical specimen
questions.correct_answer: A duplicate specimen of the holotype, collected at the same time from the same plant
questions.explanation: Isotypes are exact duplicates of the holotype, often distributed to different herbaria.

questions.question: What does the 'Principle of Priority' in botanical nomenclature state?
options: The earliest validly published name for a taxon takes precedence over later synonyms
The most recently published name is always preferred
The name chosen by the majority of botanists is correct
Names given by the original country of discovery take precedence
questions.correct_answer: The earliest validly published name for a taxon takes precedence over later synonyms
questions.explanation: Priority dates from Linnaeus's Species Plantarum (1753) for most plant groups, and the first validly published name is generally the correct one.

questions.question: What year is the starting point for priority of most plant scientific names under the ICN?
questions.explanation: 1753, the publication year of Linnaeus's Species Plantarum, is the starting point for botanical nomenclature priority for seed plants and most other groups.

questions.question: What is a 'synonym' in botanical nomenclature?
options: A different scientific name that has been applied to the same taxon
A shortened form of the accepted name
The common name of a plant
A name used only in one country
questions.correct_answer: A different scientific name that has been applied to the same taxon
questions.explanation: Synonyms are alternative names for the same taxon; only one is normally treated as the currently accepted (correct) name.

questions.question: What is a 'homonym' in nomenclature?
options: The same name applied independently to two different taxa
Two different names for the same taxon
A name spelled the same in two languages
A genus name that sounds like a family name
questions.correct_answer: The same name applied independently to two different taxa
questions.explanation: Homonyms are identical names given to different taxa; only the earliest validly published homonym can be used, later ones are illegitimate.

questions.question: Why is a name such as 'Malus Mill.' considered invalid as an epithet like 'Malus malus'?
options: It would be a tautonym, which is not permitted under the ICN for plants
It sounds unscientific
It has no author citation
It is too short
questions.correct_answer: It would be a tautonym, which is not permitted under the ICN for plants
questions.explanation: Unlike zoological nomenclature, the ICN prohibits tautonyms (identical genus and species names) for plants.

questions.question: What is the correct way to abbreviate a genus name after it has already been used once in a text, e.g. for Zea mays repeated later?
options: Z. mays
ZM
Z mays (no period)
Zea m.
questions.correct_answer: Z. mays
questions.explanation: After first full use, the genus is conventionally abbreviated to its initial letter followed by a period, e.g. Z. mays.

questions.question: What does 'sp.' following a genus name (e.g. Ficus sp.) indicate?
options: An unidentified species within that genus
A subspecies
A hybrid species
A cultivated variety
questions.correct_answer: An unidentified species within that genus
questions.explanation: 'sp.' (plural 'spp.') indicates the specific species is not identified or specified.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation 'var.' denote in a plant name such as Brassica oleracea var. capitata?
options: Variety, an infraspecific taxonomic rank
A variant spelling of the species name
A hybrid variety
The author's variation on the original description
questions.correct_answer: Variety, an infraspecific taxonomic rank
questions.explanation: 'var.' denotes a variety, a formal rank below subspecies used for naming plants with minor but consistent differences.

questions.question: What does 'subsp.' (or 'ssp.') denote in botanical nomenclature?
options: Subspecies, an infraspecific rank above variety
A subgenus
An informal common name
A synonym of the species
questions.correct_answer: Subspecies, an infraspecific rank above variety
questions.explanation: Subspecies is a formal infraspecific rank used for geographically or morphologically distinct populations within a species.

questions.question: How is a plant hybrid between two species conventionally indicated in its scientific name?
options: With a multiplication sign (×) before the epithet or between the parent names
With the word 'hybridus' added at the end
With a plus sign (+) before the genus
With an asterisk (*) after the genus
questions.correct_answer: With a multiplication sign (×) before the epithet or between the parent names
questions.explanation: The ICN uses the multiplication sign to denote hybrid origin, e.g. Mentha × piperita.

questions.question: What is meant by 'valid publication' of a plant name under the ICN?
options: Publication that meets all the Code's formal requirements, such as a Latin or English description and designation of a type
Publication in any peer-reviewed scientific journal
Any mention of the name in a textbook
Registration of the name with a government agency
questions.correct_answer: Publication that meets all the Code's formal requirements, such as a Latin or English description and designation of a type
questions.explanation: Valid publication requires meeting specific formal criteria in the Code, including effective publication, a description or diagnosis, and type designation.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'effective publication' and 'valid publication' of a name?
options: Effective publication concerns how the work was distributed; valid publication concerns whether the name meets the Code's naming requirements
They are exactly the same requirement
Effective publication applies only to fungi
Valid publication applies only to cultivated plants
questions.correct_answer: Effective publication concerns how the work was distributed; valid publication concerns whether the name meets the Code's naming requirements
questions.explanation: Effective publication relates to the medium and distribution of the publication, while valid publication additionally requires the name to satisfy nomenclatural formalities.

questions.question: Why are common names generally considered unsuitable for precise scientific communication about plants?
options: They vary between languages and regions and may refer to different species
They are always longer than scientific names
They cannot be translated into Latin
They are banned by the ICN
questions.correct_answer: They vary between languages and regions and may refer to different species
questions.explanation: A single common name can refer to different species in different regions, and one species may have many common names, causing confusion that binomials avoid.

questions.question: What is the main advantage of using Latin (or Latinized) forms for scientific names?
options: Latin is a stable, universally used language not tied to any single living nation, avoiding bias and enabling international use
Latin words are always shorter
Latin is easier to pronounce than English
Latin was the first language used by plant collectors
questions.correct_answer: Latin is a stable, universally used language not tied to any single living nation, avoiding bias and enabling international use
questions.explanation: Using a 'dead' language avoids the political and linguistic bias of adopting a living national language and gives global stability to names.

questions.question: What is a 'cultivar' in the naming of cultivated plants?
options: A plant variant maintained in cultivation through selective propagation, named under a separate cultivar code
Any wild population of a species
A synonym for subspecies
A hybrid produced only in a laboratory
questions.correct_answer: A plant variant maintained in cultivation through selective propagation, named under a separate cultivar code
questions.explanation: Cultivars are governed by the International Code of Nomenclature for Cultivated Plants, with names written in single quotes, e.g. Rosa 'Peace'.

questions.question: How is a cultivar name typically written, e.g. for a rose cultivar called Peace?
options: Rosa 'Peace'
Rosa peace
ROSA PEACE
Rosa Peace (italicized)
questions.correct_answer: Rosa 'Peace'
questions.explanation: Cultivar epithets are capitalized, not italicized, and enclosed in single quotation marks after the genus (or species) name.

questions.question: What does the abbreviation 'cf.' mean when used in a provisional identification such as Ficus cf. exasperata?
options: The specimen is tentatively identified but not fully confirmed as that species
The specimen is definitely that species
The specimen is a hybrid
The specimen was collected close to a known population
questions.correct_answer: The specimen is tentatively identified but not fully confirmed as that species
questions.explanation: 'cf.' (confer) indicates the identification is uncertain and the specimen only resembles the named species.

questions.question: In the name Vigna unguiculata (L.) Walp., what does the bracketed author citation '(L.)' indicate?
options: Linnaeus originally described the species under a different name, and Walpers later transferred it to its current genus
Linnaeus and Walpers co-published the name together
Linnaeus's description was rejected
The species was first found in Linnaeus's home country
questions.correct_answer: Linnaeus originally described the species under a different name, and Walpers later transferred it to its current genus
questions.explanation: A bracketed author citation shows the original author of the basionym, while the author outside the bracket made the later combination.

questions.question: What is a 'basionym'?
options: The original name on which a new combination or name change is based
The final accepted name of a taxon after all revisions
A name proposed but never published
The vernacular root of a scientific name
questions.correct_answer: The original name on which a new combination or name change is based
questions.explanation: A basionym is the earlier legitimate name that provides the epithet used when a taxon is transferred to a new genus or rank.

questions.question: What is the taxonomic rank immediately above Genus in the standard hierarchy?
options: Family
Order
Class
Species
questions.correct_answer: Family
questions.explanation: Family sits directly above genus: Species < Genus < Family < Order < Class < Division/Phylum < Kingdom.

questions.question: Which of these is an example of a correctly formatted botanical binomial?
options: Mangifera indica
mangifera Indica
MANGIFERA INDICA
Mangifera Indica
questions.correct_answer: Mangifera indica
questions.explanation: Only the genus is capitalized; the specific epithet is always lowercase, and both are italicized.

questions.question: What is the main function of a taxonomic key in plant identification?
options: To guide a user through a series of choices between contrasting characters to identify a plant's name
To list all plants alphabetically by common name
To record the geographic distribution of a species
To store DNA barcode sequences
questions.correct_answer: To guide a user through a series of choices between contrasting characters to identify a plant's name
questions.explanation: A dichotomous key presents paired, contrasting statements (couplets) that lead the user step by step to a correct identification.

questions.question: What is an 'illegitimate name' under the ICN?
options: A validly published name that nevertheless contravenes certain Code rules, such as being a later homonym
Any name not written in Latin
A name published without any author
A common name mistakenly used as scientific
questions.correct_answer: A validly published name that nevertheless contravenes certain Code rules, such as being a later homonym
questions.explanation: An illegitimate name is validly published but rejected for use because it violates specific nomenclatural rules (e.g., later homonymy, superfluous naming).

questions.question: In the taxonomic hierarchy, what rank lies directly between Class and Family?
options: Order
Genus
Division
Kingdom
questions.correct_answer: Order
questions.explanation: The sequence descending is Class > Order > Family, so Order sits between Class and Family.

questions.question: Why did Linnaeus's binomial system replace older, purely descriptive polynomial (multi-word) plant names?
options: Polynomials were long, unstandardized descriptive phrases that were cumbersome to use and compare
Polynomials were considered religiously inappropriate
Polynomials could not be translated into Latin at all
Polynomials were reserved only for animals
questions.correct_answer: Polynomials were long, unstandardized descriptive phrases that were cumbersome to use and compare
questions.explanation: Pre-Linnaean names were often lengthy Latin descriptive phrases; the two-word binomial offered a short, stable, standardized alternative.
